convolution.title: Convolution: the moving overlap
convolution.subtitle: A rectangle convolved with a decaying exponential. Move t and watch the overlap area become y(t).

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: x(t) is a unit rectangle on [-0.5, 0.5]; h(t) = e^'{'-t'}'u(t).
controls.timeHint: Move the reversed kernel across the input.

plot.overlapDescription: The shaded region is the integrand; its area is the output at this t.
plot.outputDescription: The marker follows the area under the product as t moves.

steps.title: Four operations
steps.shift: Shift by t to obtain h(t−τ).

observe.title: What to notice
observe.noOverlap: Before t = −0.5 the signals never overlap, so the output stays zero.
observe.rising: Between −0.5 and 0.5 the overlap grows: the output rises like 1 − e^'{'−(t+0.5)'}'.
observe.falling: After 0.5 the overlap shrinks and the output decays exponentially.
observe.area: Convolution is not pointwise multiplication; it accumulates area over the whole overlap.

sampling.title: Sampling and aliasing
sampling.subtitle: Sample a cosine at different rates. Below the Nyquist rate, a fast signal leaves a slow-looking set of samples.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: x(t) = cos(2π f₀ t), sampled every T_s = 1/f_s seconds.
controls.signalHint: The physical frequency you want to capture.
controls.samplingHint: The number of samples taken per second.

readouts.aliasHint: The low-frequency cosine that fits the same samples.

plot.title: Continuous signal, samples and alias
plot.description: Dots are the samples the system actually sees. The dashed curve is an alias that passes through the same dots.

theory.title: Why aliasing happens
theory.nyquist: A real sinusoid is uniquely determined by samples only when f_s > 2f₀. The threshold 2f₀ is the Nyquist rate.
theory.overlap: Sampling multiplies by an impulse train, which copies the spectrum every f_s. When copies overlap, high frequencies fold down.
theory.edge: At exactly f_s = 2f₀ the samples determine the frequency but not the phase, so this is a boundary case rather than a comfortable design point.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.lowRate: Set f_s to 6 Hz with f₀ = 5 Hz. Predict the apparent frequency before looking at the readout.
experiment.increase: Raise f_s above 10 Hz and watch the alias disappear.
experiment.compare: Compare the number of samples per period with the visual smoothness of the reconstruction.
experiment.question: If the samples alone are given, can you tell 5 Hz from 7 Hz at f_s = 12 Hz?

fourierSeries.title: Fourier series: from sine waves to a square wave
fourierSeries.subtitle: A square wave is an infinite sum of odd harmonics. Increase N and watch the edges sharpen while the ripple stays.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: The fundamental is 1 Hz. Only odd harmonics contribute.
controls.harmonicsHint: N is always odd; the slider adds two harmonics at a time.

readouts.overshootHint: Above the ideal square-wave level of 1

plot.timeDescription: The dashed line is the ideal square wave; the solid line is the finite partial sum.

insight.title: What the spectrum tells you
insight.odd: The square wave has odd symmetry, so only sine terms with odd k survive.
insight.decay: Harmonic amplitude falls as 1/k: high frequencies are present, but progressively weaker.
insight.gibbs: Near a jump the partial sum overshoots by about 9% and the overshoot does not vanish as N grows.
insight.convergence: More harmonics reduce the transition width, so the approximation converges in energy even though the pointwise error at the jump does not go away.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.step: Set N = 1 and notice that the result is just a sine wave.
experiment.observe: Increase N to 31 and watch the edge get steeper while the ripple remains.
experiment.spectrum: Predict the amplitude of the 9th harmonic before checking the spectrum.

firstOrder.title: First-order systems: the time constant
firstOrder.subtitle: A first-order step response reaches 63.2% at one time constant, 95% at three, and is essentially settled at five.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: K is the DC gain and τ sets how fast the system responds.
controls.gainHint: The final value of the step response.
controls.timeConstantHint: Larger τ means a slower system.

readouts.settlingHint: Within about 1% of the final value

plot.title: Step response
plot.description: The horizontal dashed line is the final value K = {value}.

insight.title: Why 63.2%?
insight.definition: τ is the time for the response to cover 1 − e^'{'−1'}' ≈ 63.2% of the remaining distance to the final value.
insight.meaning: At t = τ the slope has already fallen to 1/e of its initial value, so the response visibly slows down.
insight.bandwidth: A slower time response means a narrower bandwidth: f_c = 1/(2πτ).
insight.gain: K scales the whole response vertically; it does not change the settling time.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.changeTau: Double τ and observe that the 63.2% point moves to the right.
experiment.changeGain: Change K and confirm that the shape stays the same while the final value scales.
experiment.readPoint: Read y at τ, 2τ and 3τ, then compare with the readouts.
experiment.connect: Connect the cutoff frequency to the time constant: smaller τ means wider bandwidth.

tasks.L1-1: Build a time array and generate sine, step, exponential and triangular signals. Write your own cosine and rectangle expressions. Compare time transformations and check finite-pulse areas with midpoint sums.
tasks.L1-2: Implement three systems and both operation paths. Change inputs and coefficients, compute differences and find counterexamples. Explain why finitely many zero differences do not prove a property.
tasks.L1-3: Compute zero-input, zero-state and total responses. Change the initial state and input switch, read specified times and verify the sum of components.
tasks.L1-4: Generate rectangle and exponential responses, apply np.convolve and multiply by the time step. Construct the output time axis, implement overlap-area calculations and compare errors after halving the step.
tasks.L2-1: Sum odd sine harmonics in a loop. Compare term counts, highest frequencies and overshoot for K=1, 3, 7 and 15. Distinguish harmonic order from number of terms.
tasks.L2-2: Generate a rectangular pulse and approximate its continuous Fourier integral with an FFT. Compare the analytic spectrum while changing width, amplitude and delay. Check scaling and avoid phase readings at spectral zeros.
tasks.L2-3: Generate a 100 Hz plus 1000 Hz input, solve the continuous low-pass system with SciPy and fit amplitudes and phases over 0.1–0.2 s. Select a cutoff using both specifications.
tasks.L2-4: Generate cosine samples at explicit sampling times and apply finite sinc interpolation. Change sampling rates and candidate frequencies, find matching samples and distinguish aliasing from edge truncation.
tasks.L3-1: Generate exponential, delayed-step and rectangular signals. Numerically integrate at several s points within a convergence region and compare with your own derivations. Extend the window to assess truncation.
tasks.L3-2: Derive the zero-state response first, solve the differential equation with solve_ivp, measure y(1) and the 90% rise time, then add your analytic curve and compare errors.
tasks.L3-3: Solve the zero-input, zero-state and total responses for three initial states. Check starting values and decomposition errors and explain the initial-condition term in your derivation.
tasks.L3-4: Generate pulses with different durations and solve each output in smooth segments. Add your own candidates near the threshold and record failures and successes. Justify the shortest duration using a derivation and parameter resolution.
